title: Mega Backdoor Roth via Solo 401(k)
summary: If your Solo 401(k) provider supports after-tax contributions plus in-plan Roth conversions, you can fill up to ~$45,500 of additional Roth space.
detailsHtml:
Provider selection matters

Most discount-brokerage Solo 401(k)s (Fidelity, Schwab, Vanguard's standard offering) do NOT support after-tax contributions or in-plan Roth conversions, so they cannot facilitate the Mega Backdoor Roth. Specialized providers — MySolo401k, Solo401k.com, RocketDollar — offer customized plans that do, for setup costs of $500–$1,000 and annual fees of $150–$300. The tax savings typically justify the costs within 1–2 years for high-income contractors.

Solo 401(k)s bypass ACP testing because there are no non-HCE employees to discriminate against — you're the only participant. This is a meaningful structural advantage over employer-plan Mega Backdoor Roth, where ACP testing routinely constrains how much HCEs can fill after-tax. The full §415(c) headroom ($72,000 minus your employee deferral and any employer profit-sharing) is generally usable in a Solo 401(k).
Notice 2014-54 ordering applies in Solo 401(k)s too. The earnings on after-tax contributions are ordinary-income taxable at conversion (IRS Notice 2014-54). Configure your provider to perform automatic in-plan Roth conversion on every contribution (same-day or daily sweep) rather than quarterly or annual manual conversion. Even one-month accumulation periods leak earnings to ordinary rates for participants filling the full after-tax window.
